title: Do People Really Run Off to Join the French Foreign Legion?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a plug for the Science Channel TV show's final marathon, then do a podcast episode on the French Foreign Legion: its founding in 1831 under King Louis Philippe, its Algerian headquarters, its Mexico campaign (1861-1865), the mandatory assumed-name (nom de guerre) policy until 2010, the rules on uniforms, bank accounts and marriage during the first year, pay and contracts, the 2012 Vanity Fair article "The Expendables," the Spanish Legion comparison, and a comparison to the US. The episode ends with a listener mail from Donato about autopsies and the cause versus manner of death distinction, plus sign-off.
topics: cause of death vs manner of death

segments.title: Science Channel marathon promo and show intro
segments.summary: Josh promotes the final marathon of the Science Channel TV show, including airing dates, Amazon/iTunes availability, and a request to post on the Science Channel Facebook page. Chuck and Josh then open the podcast, joking about approaching storms.

segments.title: Van Damme and the French Foreign Legion overview
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the French Foreign Legion as a military force, joking that Jean-Claude Van Damme played a legionnaire in a movie. They discuss the kepi cap and note the Legion's long stationing in Algeria, where its headquarters was from near its founding, and its current size of about 7,000 legionnaires with around 30,000 deaths in battle.

segments.title: Legion's combat record and Mexico intervention
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Legion as a special forces unit that admits no women and has fought in nearly every French conflict since 1830. They cover the Legion's invasion of Mexico from 1861 to 1865, which installed Austrian prince Maximilian as a French-backed ruler.

segments.title: Founding in 1831 after the July Revolution
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Legion was founded after the 1830 July Revolution that replaced Charles X with Louis Philippe. Louis Philippe, wary of radical former soldiers who had helped bring him to power, created a foreign legion of foreign nationals and sent it away from France. His eight articles set the Legion's rules, traditions, and recruiting criteria.

segments.title: Recruitment rules and the assumed-name policy
segments.summary: Early recruitment required a birth certificate, good conduct papers, and a military reference, though the commandant could waive these. This led to the nom de guerre practice, where recruits joined under an assumed name. It was mandatory until 2010, when recruits could later regularize their papers and return to their old names.

segments.title: First-year restrictions, citizenship, and recruitment of criminals
segments.summary: The hosts describe restrictions during a legionnaire's first year: no civilian bank account, marriage, civilian clothes, car purchase, or foreign travel besides France. They note that married men must enlist as single, that the Legion historically accepted serious criminals but is now more selective, and that non-French nationals can gain French citizenship after three years of good standing. Recent rules now allow French nationals to join.

segments.title: Modern Legion: Vanity Fair article, pay, contracts, and Spanish Legion
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a December 2012 Vanity Fair article, The Expendables, about the Legion's current work, including fighting illicit gold miners in Guiana as Afghanistan winds down. They cover pay for a corporal, the five-year initial contract, later contracts of six months to five years, and the Legion's view of death and honor. They mention the Spanish Legion and float the idea of a US foreign legion.

segments.title: Off-topic banter on 1980s caps and brand names
segments.summary: The hosts chat about 1980s fashion, including painter's caps and bicycle caps, and try to recall a bicycle component brand, eventually landing on Shimano. They also mention where to find more on the Legion.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: A brief sponsor message is read.

segments.title: Listener mail from Donato on autopsies
segments.summary: Donato, a law enforcement worker, writes about the earlier autopsy episode, mentioning vitreous fluid extraction and toxicology results. He also explains that cause of death is the physiological mechanism while manner of death is the circumstance such as homicide. The hosts thank him and mention listener mail options.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts give contact information and sign off.
